extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, PR students, communications managers, and organizational executives
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for managing relations with traditional and new media, representing organizations publicly, and using social media and citizen journalism to build organization–public relationships. Covers ethical, tactical, and cross-cultural considerations for spokespersons and PR professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in social media / do not withhold information
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization cannot hide or withhold information in the social media environment; failure to disclose in social media campaigns damages the organization–public relationship and erodes credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open and disclose information appropriately in social media. Studies show nondisclosure harms relationships and credibility. Avoid strategies that attempt to conceal facts in social media channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate and integrate communication functions (one voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal and external communication programs must use the same message strategy; companies often put all communication functions under a single C-suite executive to ensure one voice, especially in crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure alignment across silos because search engines and publics will access all available sources. Centralize message strategy and spokesperson roles to avoid contradictory messaging; critical in crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with nontraditional gatekeepers (bloggers) and respect their expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must work with bloggers and other nontraditional media players who can shape an organization’s digital environment; bloggers often expect higher transparency and access than traditional media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize bloggers as credentialed media in many contexts; monitor the blogosphere and engage appropriately. Balance PR desire for control with bloggers’ expectations for access and transparency; create strategies for both attracting blog coverage and running organization-owned blogs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and respond to citizen journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone with a camera phone can report news; citizen journalism via cell phones and the Internet can break news faster than traditional media and can inform communities during crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor fast-breaking social channels (e.g., Twitter) and be prepared to respond quickly and accurately. Use citizen reports as both potential sources and items requiring verification; plan rapid-response protocols for incidents captured by the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social media to build two-way organization–public relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media facilitate interactive communication (two-way), build communities, empower stakeholders, and allow practitioners to engage stakeholders rather than simply “telling and selling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design social media strategies that encourage dialogue and stakeholder participation. Examples: segmenting followers by interest (Twitter), engaging volunteers on Facebook pages, creating employee social networks to reduce isolation. Expect evolution and unexpected directions in social media initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and adapt to each medium’s content, style, audience, and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing how to work with each medium—create content for each, address each medium’s audiences, adhere to specific style requirements, and meet the deadlines of each—is a major part of practitioners’ jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor content format and style (headlines, length, jargon) to each outlet. Learn lead times, submission formats, and audience expectations; timely delivery is critical, particularly for broadcast and online media with tight deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and maintain relationships of mutual respect and trust with journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must build and maintain relationships of mutual respect and trust with media gatekeepers; credibility is the practitioner’s most important asset in dealing with the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earn trust over time by being reliable, honest, and helpful. Protect reporters’ scoops and avoid favoritism among outlets. Recognize the mutual but sometimes adversarial dependence between PR and journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shoot straight (honesty and credibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Honesty is the best policy in dealing with the media; credibility must be earned and means never lying. If you can’t speak the truth for legitimate reasons, say nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lie; be transparent with both good and bad news since honesty builds long-term trust. Do not favor one news outlet over others for spot news; respect reporters’ rights to their scoops. Example anti-pattern: giving partial truths or misleading statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give service to journalists (be a reporter’s reporter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide newsworthy, interesting, and timely stories and pictures when reporters want them and in a form they can readily use. Ask enough questions to understand the reporter’s story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and meet media deadlines; provide usable formats (photos, bios, quotes). Be on call for breaking needs, keep key materials accessible, and prepare complete information to speed journalists’ work. Example: sending transcripts or polished quotes for quick web publication can be helpful but ensure expert credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not beg or whine to get coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid begging journalists to use stories or complaining about coverage; if information is not newsworthy, begging won't change that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume materials were received unless told otherwise; persistent follow-up asking 'Did you receive my release?' irritates editors. Pressuring editorial staff or threatening advertising withdrawal is unprofessional and counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ask journalists to 'kill' a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have no right to ask journalists to suppress or kill a story; such requests are unprofessional and an abuse of press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid requests to suppress coverage; instead prevent situations that produce negative stories. Legitimate requests for publication delay may be appropriate for operational security or public safety (e.g., military operations, homeland security) but should be used sparingly and with established trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not flood the media (respect newsworthiness and targeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid blanketing media with irrelevant releases; stick to what journalists will consider news, keep media lists current, and send to the single most appropriate journalist at each outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target releases to appropriate beats and outlets. Overloading newsrooms with irrelevant materials erodes credibility. Maintain curated lists and avoid mass blasts that waste editors’ time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk from the public’s interest, not the organization’s
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame communications from the viewpoint of the public’s interest rather than only the organization’s self-interest to increase relevance and trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present motives and actions in terms of public benefit (e.g., environmental or community advantages) rather than purely promotional claims. This improves newsworthiness and receptivity among journalists and publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make news easy to read and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short, punchy headlines; avoid jargon, unfamiliar acronyms, and technical terms; include personal pronouns, names, quotations, and contact information at the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format press materials for immediate usability: clear headline, lead paragraph with key fact, contact name, email, and phone. Tailor copy to reporters’ needs and provide quotable sound bites and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attempting 'off the record' statements; if you don’t want it quoted, don’t say it
rubrics_metrics.description: Spokespersons should avoid talking 'off the record' because bloggers and some new media sources may not observe traditional rules; it is too late to qualify something as off the record after saying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume anything you say can be used; train spokespeople to avoid casual comments that could be reported. Do not rely on informal off-the-record understandings with nontraditional media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with the most important fact (inverted pyramid)
rubrics_metrics.description: State the most important fact at the beginning; reporters want the decision or headline first, with supporting facts and examples following.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a first-level summary statement (short) then a second-level concrete example as evidence. If pressed, return to the summary. Prepare succinct opening statements for interviews and releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain composure and do not argue with reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not argue with a reporter or lose your cool; journalists will pursue stories and may push hard to get information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep responses professional and measured. Avoid confrontation that can produce negative sound bites; preserve relationships even when coverage is unfavorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not repeat offensive language in questions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a question contains offensive language or words you dislike, do not repeat them even to deny them, because reporters can select quotes and words for final stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refuse to restate or repeat inflammatory phrasing; instead reframe answers using neutral language. Be concise on tough questions to avoid offering quotable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give direct answers to direct questions; keep tough answers short
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reporter asks a direct question, give an equally direct answer (yes/no when appropriate) and say no more; tougher questions deserve shorter answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist pressure to volunteer extra information; if a reporter falls silent after an answer, do not fill the silence. Treat camera/microphone as always on; prepare short, accurate responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you don’t know, say so and promise to follow up
rubrics_metrics.description: If spokespersons do not know the answer, they should say, 'I don’t know, but I’ll get the answer for you,' and then follow through promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate questions in advance, prepare succinct answers, and rehearse with mock interviews. Track promised follow-ups and deliver them quickly to maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the truth, even if it hurts; treat bad news like any other story
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the truth, even if it hurts; prepare bad news as if it were good news and take it to the media to maintain control and avoid appearing to hide facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early and honest disclosure of adverse events builds trust and reduces vulnerability to accusations of concealment. Convince management that transparency is the better long-term strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call a news conference only when reporters consider it newsworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not call a news conference unless you have what reporters consider news; use news conferences when reporters need an opportunity to ask questions (e.g., complex matters requiring backgrounding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate alternatives before convening a press conference; reserve them for timely breaking matters or complex announcements where Q&A and backgrounding are necessary. If holding one, apply the other guidelines (honesty, brevity, preparation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt media relations for international contexts (language, culture, politics)
rubrics_metrics.description: When working with news media from other countries, follow the basic principles but also account for linguistic, cultural, and political differences; media systems vary (authoritarian, communist, revolutionary, western, developmental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate documents into appropriate language variants (e.g., distinct Chinese character sets), avoid culturally insulting language or superlatives that may offend, and include local sources and information. Tailor messaging to the local media system and sensitivities.

rubrics_metrics.name: View media relations as an investment in accuracy and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Media relations should be seen as an investment: accuracy and fairness in press coverage result from both reporters’ work and the quality of the practitioner–journalist relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in building long-term credibility and professional relationships to improve coverage accuracy. Provide reliable information and facilitate journalism rather than attempting to manipulate coverage.
